items.question: According to EASA rules, who is responsible for the safe operation of the AW189 and has final authority as to the disposition of the helicopter?
options: The operator's managing director.
The aircraft commander (pilot-in-command).
The air traffic controller providing service.
The maintenance organisation.
items.explanation: EASA Air Ops and Air Crew rules state that the pilot-in-command has the final authority and responsibility for the safe operation of the aircraft.

items.question: Under EASA rules, when may the pilot-in-command deviate from rules and procedures when operating the AW189?
options: Never, rules must always be followed.
Only with written permission from the operator.
Only when such deviation is absolutely necessary in the interest of safety.
Only after informing ATC in writing.
items.explanation: Air Law permits the PIC to deviate from rules and procedures only to the extent necessary for the safety of the flight.
references: EASA Air Ops — Deviation from rules

items.question: Before commencing an IFR flight with the AW189, which of the following is an EASA requirement regarding weather and aerodromes?
options: Destination aerodrome must always be VFR only.
At least one destination or alternate must have weather above operating minima for the expected time of use.
No weather information is required if the helicopter has de-icing.
Only wind information is required.
items.explanation: IFR planning requires that weather at destination or alternate be at or above the applicable minima at the expected time of use.

items.question: Which of the following best describes an EASA requirement for fuel planning for an IFR AW189 offshore flight?
options: Fuel for taxi only.
Fuel for take-off and climb only.
Fuel to destination, approach, missed approach (if required), alternate (if required) and final reserve.
Fuel to destination only, as alternates are not considered.
items.explanation: IFR fuel planning must ensure sufficient fuel for all phases including alternate and final reserve, with additional considerations for offshore operations.

items.question: Under EASA rules, when is the carriage of a CVR and FDR typically required for an AW189?
options: Never for rotorcraft.
Only for single-pilot VFR flights.
For multi-pilot commercial air transport operations of this mass category as specified in the regulations.
Only when carrying dangerous goods.
items.explanation: CVR/FDR requirements depend on aircraft mass, crew and operation type; the AW189, as a large multi-pilot commercial transport helicopter, is typically required to carry both.

items.question: Under EASA rules, what is the primary purpose of the operator's Operations Manual (OM) for AW189 operations?
options: Provide advertising material.
Specify standard operating procedures, responsibilities and policies for safe operation.
Replace all regulatory requirements.
Serve only as maintenance instructions.
items.explanation: The OM sets out company procedures, responsibilities and policies that must comply with regulations and support safe operation.

items.question: What is a general EASA requirement regarding duty and rest times for flight crew operating the AW189?
options: There are no limits for helicopter crews.
Maximum duty periods and minimum rest times are defined to prevent fatigue.
Duty times are determined only by the pilot.
Only cabin crew are subject to limits.
items.explanation: Flight and duty time limitations and rest requirements exist to mitigate fatigue risks for flight crew.

items.question: What is the pilot-in-command's obligation regarding compliance with ATC clearances during IFR AW189 operations?
options: Clearances may be ignored for convenience.
Clearances must be complied with unless safety requires deviation, in which case ATC must be informed as soon as practicable.
Only altitude clearances are mandatory.
Only heading clearances are mandatory.
items.explanation: PIC must normally comply with ATC clearances but may deviate if safety demands; ATC must be informed when possible.

items.question: According to EASA, when must the AW189 be equipped with transponder and altitude reporting capability?
options: Only in uncontrolled airspace.
When operating in airspace or on routes where SSR transponder with altitude reporting is mandated.
Never, helicopters are exempt.
Only at night.
items.explanation: Use of SSR transponders with altitude reporting is required in specified airspace and on specified routes.

items.question: What is a basic requirement for VFR visibility and distance from cloud when operating the AW189 in controlled airspace below 10 000 ft AMSL (non-special VFR)?
options: No visibility is required.
3 km visibility and clear of cloud.
5 km visibility and prescribed distances from cloud depending on class of airspace.
Only distance from terrain is specified.
items.explanation: EASA rules define minimum flight visibility and separation from cloud varying with airspace class; typically at least 5 km below 10 000 ft in controlled airspace.

items.question: What is the general rule for right-of-way when two aircraft are converging at approximately the same altitude?
options: The slower aircraft has right-of-way.
The aircraft on the right has right-of-way.
The heavier aircraft has right-of-way.
Helicopters always have right-of-way.
items.explanation: Standard rules of the air state that the aircraft to the other's right has right-of-way in converging situations, with some exceptions.

items.question: What is the general rule for right-of-way when two aircraft are approaching head-on at similar altitude?
options: Both shall alter course to the right.
Both shall alter course to the left.
The bigger aircraft has priority.
The smaller aircraft has priority.
items.explanation: Head-on approaches require both aircraft to alter course to the right.

items.question: What is the minimum height for IFR en-route flight over non-mountainous terrain according to common EASA practice, unless otherwise specified?
options: At least 200 ft above any obstacle within 8 km.
At least 1000 ft above the highest obstacle within 8 km of the estimated position.
At least 10 000 ft regardless of obstacles.
No minimum is required.
items.explanation: A common requirement is 1000 ft obstacle clearance within a specified lateral distance; mountainous areas may require more. Offshore sectors are typically flown at agreed cruise levels over open water.

items.question: Under EASA rules, when is a take-off alternate required for AW189 IFR operations?
options: Never for helicopters.
When weather at departure aerodrome is below landing minima but above take-off minima.
Only for VFR flights.
Only at night.
items.explanation: If landing back at the departure aerodrome is not possible after take-off due to weather, a take-off alternate must be available.

items.question: What is the general requirement for carriage of the Operations Manual and other documents on board the AW189?
options: No documents are required.
Only the pilot's licence is required.
Documents required by regulations (AFM, OM parts, licences, etc.) must be available on board or accessible as permitted.
Only maintenance records are required.
items.explanation: Regulations specify which documents must be carried or be readily accessible for the operation.
references: EASA Air Ops — Documents to be Carried

items.question: When is the use of seat belts and, when provided, shoulder harnesses required for crew members during AW189 operations?
options: Only during take-off.
During take-off, landing and whenever deemed necessary for safety.
Only during cruise.
They are not required.
items.explanation: Crew must use belts and harnesses during critical phases and whenever safety considerations dictate.
references: EASA Air Ops — Use of Safety Belts

items.question: Under Air Law, what is the captain's responsibility regarding alcohol and psychoactive substances for AW189 crew?
options: Only passengers are subject to restrictions.
Crew must not perform duties while under the influence or within specified time after consumption.
Only cabin crew are affected.
There are no rules for helicopters.
items.explanation: Regulations prohibit crew from performing duties under the influence of alcohol or psychoactive substances and may specify time limits before duty.
references: EASA Air Ops — Alcohol and Psychoactive Substances

items.question: What is the primary purpose of a Minimum Equipment List (MEL) for AW189 operations?
options: To list the heaviest items on board.
To specify which equipment may be inoperative for dispatch and under what conditions.
To list only cabin equipment.
To replace the AFM.
items.explanation: The MEL defines dispatch conditions when certain equipment is unserviceable, ensuring an acceptable safety level.

items.question: In which situations may the AW189 pilot-in-command refuse carriage of passengers or cargo?
options: Never.
When he/she reasonably considers that safety might be endangered.
Only when the operator agrees in writing.
Only for cargo, not passengers.
items.explanation: PIC may refuse carriage if it is considered that passengers or cargo could endanger the safety of the aircraft or persons on board.

items.question: What is the normal rule regarding carriage of dangerous goods on the AW189?
options: They are always allowed without restriction.
They are only allowed if carried in accordance with technical instructions, approvals and company procedures.
They are allowed only for passengers.
They are never allowed under any circumstances.
items.explanation: Dangerous goods may be carried only when in compliance with regulations, approvals and operator procedures.
references: ICAO Technical Instructions / EASA Air Ops

items.question: For offshore helicopter operations such as those flown by the AW189, what is a general EASA requirement regarding survival equipment?
options: Life jackets and rafts are optional over water.
Approved life jackets must be worn and appropriate survival equipment carried for the route and conditions flown.
Only the commander needs a life jacket.
Survival equipment is only required at night.
items.explanation: Offshore operations rules require crew and passengers to wear approved life jackets and require appropriate survival equipment (rafts, locator beacons, etc.) to be carried, matched to the overwater segment and conditions.
references: EASA Air Ops — Operations Over Water (Offshore)

items.question: Under EASA offshore operations rules, what governs the AW189's minimum equipment and performance class when flying to an offshore helideck?
options: No specific offshore rules apply; normal onshore rules are used.
Specific offshore operations requirements (e.g. Performance Class 1 for critical phases, HEMS/offshore equipment) apply in addition to general Air Ops rules.
Only the operator's internal policy applies, with no regulatory basis.
Offshore flights are always conducted under VFR only.
items.explanation: Offshore helicopter operations are subject to additional EASA requirements (performance class, equipment, weather minima) beyond general commercial air transport rules.
references: EASA Air Ops — Offshore Operations (Part-SPO/Part-CAT Annex)
